title: Burnout and Coping Strategies among Merchant Marine Seafarers: A Systematic Review
abstract:
This systematic review examines burnout and coping strategies among merchant marine seafarers—a professional group exposed to intense psychosocial stress yet still insufficiently represented in occupational health research.

Following PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic search was conducted across six international databases (Web of Science, Scopus, PubMed, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar) covering the years 2015–2025. From 732 initially identified records, 10 studies meeting all inclusion criteria were selected. Data extraction was performed using a standardized matrix, and methodological quality was evaluated with the JBI Critical Appraisal Checklist for Analytical Cross-Sectional Studies.

The included studies consistently report moderate to high levels of burnout, assessed using validated yet heterogeneous instruments (Maslach Burnout Inventory, Oldenburg Burnout Inventory, Copenhagen Burnout Inventory, Seafarers’ Exhaustion Scale, and maritime‑specific measures). Although most studies do not employ standardized coping scales (e.g., Brief COPE), they analyze various coping‑related resources such as social support, transformational leadership, resilience, sense of belonging, and organizational climate. These resources demonstrate protective effects, mitigating emotional exhaustion and depersonalization associated with high job demands. Three overarching thematic domains emerged: (1) organizational constraints (overwork, contract duration, isolation, harassment), (2) psychosocial resources (social support, leadership, psychological health climate, resilience), and (3) relational and cultural factors (sense of belonging, crew cohesion, collective values).

This review provides the first comprehensive synthesis of the relationship between burnout and coping among merchant marine seafarers. It underscores the relevance of the Job Demands–Resources model as a central explanatory framework while highlighting the lack of standardized coping assessments in maritime research. The findings emphasize the need for longitudinal and multicenter studies to empirically examine adaptive coping mechanisms in seafaring populations. By outlining the foundations for a conceptual model of maritime burnout, this review offers a robust scientific basis for developing targeted mental health prevention strategies and interventions at sea.
